docs.title: edge-rs
docs.text: edgeR's quasi-likelihood pipeline and limma-voom for Python, with the numerics in the edge-rs Rust crate. No R, no rpy2. NumPy in, polars out, and every function named after the R function it reproduces.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
uv pip install edge-rs

The runtime dependencies are NumPy, polars and beartype. That's it.

docs.title: Thirty seconds
docs.text:
import edge_rs

# counts: (n_genes, n_samples), as in edgeR
res = edge_rs.run_edger_ql(counts, design, feature_ids=genes, coef="treated")
res = edge_rs.run_limma_voom(counts, design, feature_ids=genes, coef="treated")

Or step by step, as in edgeR and limma:

keep = edge_rs.filter_by_expr(counts, design=design)
lib_size = counts.sum(axis=0)
nf = edge_rs.calc_norm_factors(counts[keep], lib_size=lib_size)

fit = edge_rs.glm_ql_fit(counts[keep], design, lib_size=lib_size, norm_factors=nf)
edge_rs.top_tags(edge_rs.glm_ql_ftest(fit, coef="treated"))

vfit = edge_rs.voom_lm_fit(counts[keep], design, lib_size=lib_size, norm_factors=nf)
edge_rs.top_table(edge_rs.ebayes(vfit), coef="treated")

If you would rather not carry lib_size around, make_dgelist bundles counts, library sizes, normalisation factors and annotation. Subsetting it keeps the library sizes of the full matrix, as edgeR's keep.lib.sizes = TRUE does, and every function above takes it in place of the counts:

dge = edge_rs.make_dgelist(counts, genes=pl.DataFrame({"gene_id": genes}))
dge = edge_rs.calc_norm_factors(dge[edge_rs.filter_by_expr(dge, design=design)])
fit = edge_rs.glm_ql_fit(dge, design)
edge_rs.top_tags(
    edge_rs.glm_ql_ftest(fit, coef="treated"), feature_ids=dge.genes["gene_id"]
)

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Counts are genes x samples. Single cell tools are the other way round; hand over x.T. Non-contiguous arrays are fine.
  • A design is a NumPy matrix or a polars frame. With a frame, the column names become coefficient names and coef="treated" works.
  • Everything is 0-based. Coefficients by position, feature_id when you pass no ids.
  • Results are polars frames with snake_case columns (log_fc, p_value, fdr, adj_p_value). top_tags and top_table sort as R does; the pipelines keep the input order.

docs.title: How close to R?
docs.text: The Rust crate is checked against edgeR 4.8.2 and limma 3.66.0 on committed fixtures, and the Python test suite runs the same fixtures through the bindings. Filtering, TMM, CPM, the QL F-test, voom, eBayes(), contrasts.fit() and topTable() all match to the tolerances in the crate's end-to-end tests.

docs.title: Filtering and normalisation
docs.text:
edgeR and limma-voom differential expression, in Rust.

NumPy in, polars out. Counts are (n_genes, n_samples) as in edgeR, every index is 0-based, and a design is a NumPy matrix or a polars frame whose column names become coefficient names.

One call:

>>> res = edge_rs.run_edger_ql(counts, design, feature_ids=genes, coef="treated")
>>> res = edge_rs.run_limma_voom(counts, design, feature_ids=genes, coef="treated")

Step by step, as in edgeR and limma:

>>> keep = edge_rs.filter_by_expr(counts, design=design)
>>> lib = counts.sum(axis=0)
>>> nf = edge_rs.calc_norm_factors(counts[keep], lib_size=lib)
>>> fit = edge_rs.glm_ql_fit(counts[keep], design, lib_size=lib, norm_factors=nf)
>>> edge_rs.top_tags(edge_rs.glm_ql_ftest(fit, coef="treated"))

Every function that takes counts also takes a DgeList from make_dgelist, which carries lib_size and norm_factors and keeps the library sizes of the full matrix through a gene subset.

docs.title: Pipelines
docs.text:
Filter, TMM, fit, test and table in one call. Worked through in Bulk differential expression and Pseudobulk with bixverse.

edgeR and limma-voom differential expression, in Rust.

NumPy in, polars out. Counts are (n_genes, n_samples) as in edgeR, every index is 0-based, and a design is a NumPy matrix or a polars frame whose column names become coefficient names.

One call:

>>> res = edge_rs.run_edger_ql(counts, design, feature_ids=genes, coef="treated")
>>> res = edge_rs.run_limma_voom(counts, design, feature_ids=genes, coef="treated")

Step by step, as in edgeR and limma:

>>> keep = edge_rs.filter_by_expr(counts, design=design)
>>> lib = counts.sum(axis=0)
>>> nf = edge_rs.calc_norm_factors(counts[keep], lib_size=lib)
>>> fit = edge_rs.glm_ql_fit(counts[keep], design, lib_size=lib, norm_factors=nf)
>>> edge_rs.top_tags(edge_rs.glm_ql_ftest(fit, coef="treated"))

Every function that takes counts also takes a DgeList from make_dgelist, which carries lib_size and norm_factors and keeps the library sizes of the full matrix through a gene subset.

docs.title: Intro¶
docs.text:
edge_rs is edgeR's quasi-likelihood pipeline and limma-voom for Python, without R. The numerics are a Rust port of both packages, checked against edgeR 4.8.2 and limma 3.66.0. The Python layer is thin on purpose: counts go in as a NumPy array, results come out as polars frames, and every function is named after the R function it reproduces. If you have run glmQLFit() or voom() before, there is nothing new to learn here.

The flow is the one from the edgeR and limma user guides:

filter_by_expr()       # drop genes too low to test
calc_norm_factors()    # TMM
  -> glm_ql_fit()   -> glm_ql_ftest()  -> top_tags()    # edgeR QL
  -> voom_lm_fit()  -> ebayes()        -> top_table()   # limma-voom

Two conventions to keep in mind throughout. Counts are genes x samples, as in R. And a design can be a plain NumPy matrix or a polars frame; with the frame, its column names become coefficient names you can test by name.

docs.title: The data¶
docs.text: The mouse mammary gland data from Fu, et al., the same data the edgeR quasi-likelihood workflow of Chen, Lun and Smyth is built on. Basal and luminal cells, sorted from virgin, pregnant and lactating mice, two replicates each: twelve samples, six groups. GEO carries the gene counts as a supplementary file, and the series matrix tells us which sample is which.

docs.title: Filtering¶
docs.text: filter_by_expr() is edgeR's filterByExpr(): keep a gene if it reaches a minimum count-per-million in enough samples to make up the smallest group. Pass the grouping (any sequence of labels, a NumPy array or a polars Series) or a design.

docs.title: Normalisation¶
docs.text: TMM normalisation factors next, on the kept genes. The one subtlety is the library size. edgeR's keep.lib.sizes = TRUE default keeps the library sizes of the full count matrix after filtering, so we pass the unfiltered column sums explicitly. Leave lib_size out and you get the column sums of whatever you hand in, which after a filter is not the same thing.

docs.title: With a DgeList¶
docs.text: If carrying lib_size around by hand sounds like a bug waiting to happen, make_dgelist() bundles counts, library sizes, normalisation factors and annotation into a frozen record, edgeR's DGEList minus the S4. Subsetting genes keeps the library sizes of the full matrix, and every function that takes counts takes a DgeList instead and reads both from it.

docs.title: A first look¶
docs.text: Before testing anything, check what separates the samples. Log-CPM via cpm(), then a PCA on the 500 most variable genes with plain NumPy.

docs.title: The design¶
docs.text: One coefficient per group, no intercept, which makes the contrasts easy to read. A polars frame keeps the column names; a NumPy matrix works as well, but then coefficients go by position only.

docs.title: edgeR quasi-likelihood¶
docs.text: glm_ql_fit() fits the negative binomial GLM per gene and squeezes the quasi-likelihood dispersions towards a trend, as edgeR 4's glmQLFit() does. No separate estimateDisp() step: since edgeR 4 the QL fit estimates what it needs itself. legacy=True gives you the old route with the trended dispersion from estimateDisp() first.

docs.title: limma-voom¶
docs.text: Same data, same design, limma's route. voom_lm_fit() is edgeR's voomLmFit(): voom's precision weights and the weighted linear model in one step, with structural zeros (a group that is all zero for a gene) handled properly. Then contrasts_fit() and ebayes(), as in limma.

docs.title: edgeR and limma side by side¶
docs.text: Two models, one question. They should agree on the big picture and differ at the margins.

docs.title: One-liners¶
docs.text: Most of the time you want the whole chain on a count matrix and nothing in between. run_edger_ql() and run_limma_voom() do filter, TMM, fit, test and table in one go, on the unfiltered counts. The defaults match the steps above, so the answers do too.

docs.title: Speed¶
docs.text: Twelve samples and 16k genes after filtering is small, and it shows.

docs.title: What is not there (yet)¶
docs.text:
The Rust crate has more than the bindings expose so far. Not in Python yet: the exact test, glmFit() / glmLRT() / glmTreat(), diffSpliceDGE(), limma's moderated F-test across several coefficients (topTableF()), duplicateCorrelation() and sample weights. NEBULA lives in bixverse, where the single cell data is.

For pseudobulk from single cell data, see the pseudobulk vignette.

docs.title: Intro¶
docs.text:
Single cell differential expression across conditions has a replication problem. Five thousand monocytes from eight donors are eight observations, not five thousand, and a test over cells pretends otherwise. Summing the counts per donor and condition (pseudobulk) and running a bulk method on the sums is the boring, honest fix, and in benchmarks it is also one of the best performing ones (Squair, et al.).

bixverse does the single cell side: QC, cell type labels, and the summing, straight off its on-disk store. edge_rs does the bulk side. The hand-off is one NumPy array and a transpose. This vignette runs it per cell type on the Kang PBMCs, with both edgeR QL and limma-voom.

docs.title: The data¶
docs.text: Kang, et al. pooled PBMCs from eight lupus donors, split each sample in two and stimulated one half with IFN-beta. Every donor contributes to both arms, which makes it a paired design. bixverse downloads the h5ad, runs its QC and writes the store into a temporary directory.

docs.title: Pseudobulking¶
docs.text: One pseudobulk sample per cell type, donor and condition. Build the groups from the obs table with polars, then hand get_pseudobulked() a dict of sample name to cell ids.

docs.title: One cell type¶
docs.text: CD14+ monocytes first. The design blocks on the donor, which is what makes it a paired test, and the coefficient of interest is stim.

docs.title: Same answer as bixverse¶
docs.text: bixverse has its own pseudobulk_dge(), which runs the same edgeR QL Rust code under the hood. It takes a cell type subset and the cell list for it. The numbers should be identical, and they are.

docs.title: Every cell type¶
docs.text: Pseudobulk once, then loop over the cell types. Each fit is a few tens of milliseconds, so the loop costs nothing next to loading the data.

docs.title: Where next¶
docs.text: Pseudobulk throws away the within-donor variability. If you want to keep the cells and model the donor as a random effect, bixverse has NEBULA; its differential expression vignette puts the two side by side. For the bulk functions in more depth, see the bulk vignette.
